Every July I watch the new international residents, and the ones who struggle are rarely the ones with weak medicine. They are the ones who go straight to the point. In this hospital, a case discussion starts with thirty seconds of small talk. Long night, wasn't it? You're on call again on Friday, aren't you? Nobody expects a real answer. It is a way of saying: I see you, and we are on the same team. The second thing is requests. If you say give me the labs, people hear an order, even if you mean it politely. Say could you send me the labs, or you couldn't send me the labs, could you? It sounds small, but the nurses will remember. And the third thing: listen for the cues. When I say let's touch base tomorrow, I am closing the conversation. When I give you a heads-up, I am telling you something important without making it dramatic. Learn those three things, and your English will sound a lot more American than your accent ever will.

In my first month I had a reputation, and I did not know it. A nurse told me later that people thought I was rude. I was surprised, because I was trying hard to be efficient. I said things like: bring me the chart, call the family, the patient in bed two needs a dressing. In my language that is normal between colleagues. Here it sounded blunt. The nurse who told me was kind about it. She gave me a heads-up over coffee, and she said: you're a good doctor, you know that, don't you? But you need to soften it a little. So I started adding could you and would you mind. I started asking the nurses about their weekends. It felt awkward for about two weeks. Then it was just how I talked. Last month a new resident asked me how I had become so popular with the nursing staff. I told him: small talk, and the word please.
